bahai.1: Seekers are welcomed with unity language, interfaith warmth, firesides and consultation.
bahai.2: Baháʼí communities may offer warmth through firesides, study circles and classes.
bahai.3: The Baháʼí Faith offers a sweeping future of world unity, peace and racial harmony.
bahai.4: Someone distancing may be gently contacted with invitations to firesides.
bahai.5: The Baháʼí Faith can devalue dissent by framing criticism as disunity, ego or impatience.
bahai.7: Investigation must arrive at the Covenant; dissent risks shunning as a covenant-breaker.
bahai.8: Service is rewarded irregularly with appointment or mention, so believers serve more.
bahai.9: A seeker is welcomed through unity, but the standard shifts to obeying administration.
bahai.10: "Independent investigation" is stressed to seekers, then covenant loyalty becomes central.
bahai.11: Baháʼí institutions may accuse critics of disunity while avoiding accountability.
bahai.12: A person questions administration, and the first response may deny coercion.
bahai.13: Service expectations become normal through study circles, teaching plans and unity.
bahai.14: Baháʼí isolation is often soft: community activities gradually become the social world.
bahai.15: Baháʼí triangulation can run through Spiritual Assemblies and the House of Justice.
bahai.16: A Baháʼí who questions administration may be approached by assembly members and friends.
bahai.17: Critics of administration may be described as disunified, ego-driven or impatient.
bahai.18: A member raises concerns and is redirected to consultation, patience and unity.
bahai.19: Seekers consent to a faith of unity, then meet administrative obedience.
bahai.20: A member feels distress when dissent threatens unity, then relief on returning to harmony.
bahai.21: A member raises concerns but is repeatedly redirected into consultation and patience.
bahai.23: Members who dissent may be treated as impatient or not understanding the Covenant.
bahai.24: The person's identity may be absorbed into unity, service, administration and the future.
bahai.26: Baháʼí financial control may appear as moral pressure to support the Faith's growth.
bahai.27: Baháʼí communities may manufacture crisis around disunity, dissent and failure to serve.
bahai.28: A member who publicly criticizes administration may be treated as disunified or immature.
bahai.29: A member who stops serving is replaced by someone eager for study circles.
bahai.30: Seekers hear of independent investigation; after enrollment dissent may meet obedience.

confucianism.1: A person is welcomed into a moral universe of order, family, respect and social harmony.
confucianism.2: Confucian systems offer social stability: family duty, elder care, education, hierarchy.
confucianism.3: Obey roles and sacrifice desire now, and the family or society will flourish later.
confucianism.4: Resisting expectations may be met with filial guilt: "After all your parents sacrificed."
confucianism.5: Confucian systems can devalue the individual beneath role: child, parent, elder, subject.
confucianism.7: The child of a harmful parent must choose between the lie that honors and the truth.
confucianism.8: Elder approval is dispensed sparingly; a lifetime of duty may earn one deathbed sentence.
confucianism.9: A child obeys parents, then obedience becomes career choice, marriage choice, elder care.
confucianism.10: "Respect" can mean courtesy, obedience, silence, or family reputation.
confucianism.11: Elders may accuse younger people of selfishness for choosing their own marriage or career.
confucianism.12: An adult child names parental control, and the family calls it love, sacrifice or duty.
confucianism.13: Children are normalized into hierarchy early: elders speak, children obey.
confucianism.14: Confucian isolation works through family hierarchy, filial piety and demands for harmony.
confucianism.15: Confucian triangulation is often family-based: parents, elders, ancestors and family name.
confucianism.16: An adult child resisting family control may be pressured by parents, elders and relatives.
confucianism.17: Adult children setting boundaries may be smeared as ungrateful, selfish or disrespectful.
confucianism.18: Adult children ask for boundaries and hear silence, shame or "after all we did for you."
confucianism.19: Adult children "choose" careers and roles after years of filial debt and guilt.
confucianism.20: Family systems can bond through guilt and relief: "After all we did for you."
confucianism.21: Adult children setting boundaries meet tears, silence, shame and charges of ingratitude.
confucianism.22: Parents control career, marriage and religion under the language of love and harmony.
confucianism.24: The person is defined by role: child, parent, spouse, elder, student, ancestor.
confucianism.26: Family financial control may appear through tuition, housing, inheritance and elder care.
confucianism.27: Families may manufacture crisis around marriage, career, elder respect and reputation.
confucianism.28: Adult children who reject expectations may meet silence, shame or inheritance threats.
confucianism.29: A noncompliant adult child is emotionally replaced by a more obedient sibling or cousin.
confucianism.30: Parents say they only advise, while money, guilt and inheritance enforce compliance.

hinduism.1: Seekers are drawn by yoga, temples, gurus, festivals and the promise all paths are valid.
hinduism.2: Temples and ashrams may provide food, festivals, community support and guru guidance.
hinduism.3: Hindu traditions can future-fake through moksha, better rebirth and guru blessing.
hinduism.4: A person leaving may be told they are abandoning dharma or creating bad karma.
hinduism.5: Hindu institutional systems can devalue through karma, caste, purity and guru hierarchy.
hinduism.6: A person questions caste or guru authority and is told they do not understand dharma.
hinduism.7: All paths are valid, but leaving this guru's path shows their karma is not ripe.
hinduism.8: Darshan is structured scarcity: long queues, brief contact, rarity as proof of potency.
hinduism.9: A person fulfills family rituals, then must also obey caste, marriage and purity rules.
hinduism.10: Caste may be called spiritual order, social custom or irrelevant ideal, by criticism.
hinduism.11: Caste-based systems may accuse lower-status people of impurity while protecting hierarchy.
hinduism.12: A person challenges caste discrimination; the response may call it culture.
hinduism.13: Family ritual, caste expectations and purity rules become normal as family life.
hinduism.14: Hindu isolation may operate through family, caste, marriage rules and temple networks.
hinduism.15: Hindu triangulation can run through parents, caste networks, gurus, astrologers, priests.
hinduism.16: A person resisting caste expectations may be pressured by parents, relatives and priests.
hinduism.17: Critics of caste may be labeled anti-Hindu, Westernized, colonized, or ignorant of dharma.
hinduism.18: A person challenges caste and is told, "This is tradition" or "do not disrespect elders."
hinduism.19: A young adult "chooses" arranged marriage after family honor and caste narrow the field.
hinduism.20: Family, caste, karma and guru authority can create cycles of shame and relief.
hinduism.21: A person challenges caste or guru authority and is told it is karma, dharma or tradition.
hinduism.22: Family control over marriage, ritual and caste may be framed as dharma and parental love.
hinduism.23: Adult children may be treated as incapable of choosing spouse or career without elders.
hinduism.24: Identity may be shaped by caste, family, gender, karma, dharma and ancestral duty.
hinduism.26: Hindu financial control can appear through temple donations, ritual fees, guru offerings.
hinduism.27: Families may manufacture crisis around marriage, caste, astrology and family honor.
hinduism.28: A person who rejects caste or guru authority may be treated as dishonoring family.
hinduism.29: A child who rejects arranged expectations may be replaced by an obedient sibling.
hinduism.30: Families call marriage choices voluntary, while caste and honor make refusal devastating.

jehovahs-witnesses.1: A lonely or grieving person receives home visits, Bible studies and patient attention.
jehovahs-witnesses.2: Witnesses may offer home visits, Bible studies, friendship and help during illness.
jehovahs-witnesses.3: Witnesses future-fake through a paradise earth: no sickness, no death, resurrection.
jehovahs-witnesses.4: When a Witness drifts, elders may visit or call; family guilt carries the rest.
jehovahs-witnesses.5: Witnesses can devalue through constant contrast with the wicked world.
jehovahs-witnesses.7: Study is mandatory but independent research is 'spiritual pornography'.
jehovahs-witnesses.8: Standing is continuously variable: commendation, privileges given and quietly removed.
jehovahs-witnesses.9: A Bible student's study grows into meetings, field service, baptism and shunning.
jehovahs-witnesses.10: "New light" lets past doctrines be mandatory then replaceable without accountability.
jehovahs-witnesses.11: Witnesses may call ex-members apostate, bitter or proud, avoiding accountability.
jehovahs-witnesses.12: A Witness questions shunning; the organization denies wrongdoing or says critics distort.
jehovahs-witnesses.13: Witnesses are normalized into meetings, field service and suspicion of "the world."
jehovahs-witnesses.14: Witnesses isolate explicitly through warnings against "the world" and apostates.
jehovahs-witnesses.15: Witnesses triangulate through elders, Governing Body, family and Armageddon fear.
jehovahs-witnesses.16: A drifting Witness may receive elder visits, family pressure and shepherding calls.
jehovahs-witnesses.17: Ex-members may be labeled apostate, mentally diseased, bitter, proud or satanic.
jehovahs-witnesses.18: A member questions failed predictions or shunning and is told to wait on Jehovah.
jehovahs-witnesses.19: A person "chooses" baptism after social life and family approval are tied to loyalty.
jehovahs-witnesses.20: Witnesses are bonded through Armageddon fear, paradise hope and shunning.
jehovahs-witnesses.21: A Witness questions doctrine and is told to wait on Jehovah and trust the Governing Body.
jehovahs-witnesses.24: Witness identity reorganizes life around meetings, service and separation from the world.
jehovahs-witnesses.26: Witnesses may use donations, unpaid construction labor and organizational volunteering.
jehovahs-witnesses.27: Witnesses may manufacture crisis through Armageddon urgency and apostate fear.

oriental-orthodoxy.4: Family and priests recall the lapsed at feasts and fasts.
oriental-orthodoxy.7: Marriage is holy, and a failed one cannot end.
oriental-orthodoxy.14: Minority identity makes the church the whole world.
oriental-orthodoxy.15: Family, priest and community align on marriage and fasting.
oriental-orthodoxy.17: Dissenting movements are labeled divisive, such as the Eritrean Sunday-school movement.
oriental-orthodoxy.20: Shared martyrdom memory binds members to the hierarchy.
oriental-orthodoxy.23: Laity defer to clergy on family decisions.
oriental-orthodoxy.26: The church takes fees, and schisms have been settled with funding.
oriental-orthodoxy.30: Patriarchates cite the state; states cite the church.

protestant-evangelical.1: The newcomer is greeted by coffee teams, worship music and instant "family" language.
protestant-evangelical.2: Evangelical churches often offer free childcare, youth groups, counseling and recovery.
protestant-evangelical.3: Evangelicalism often sells a personalized future: a plan, a calling, a breakthrough.
protestant-evangelical.4: The hoover often begins softly: "We just miss your face," "You're still family."
protestant-evangelical.5: Evangelicalism often devalues through the language of being lost, broken or backslidden.
protestant-evangelical.6: A member says, "The pastor manipulated me," and hears, "You have a critical spirit."
protestant-evangelical.7: Salvation is by grace alone, yet standing is measured by attendance and tithing.
protestant-evangelical.8: Worship delivers a Sunday high that is never reliable; failures mean "press in."
protestant-evangelical.9: Salvation is a free gift, then the believer must prove it through quiet time and giving.
protestant-evangelical.10: Churches say "relationship, not religion," but build detailed expectations.
protestant-evangelical.11: Churches accuse leavers of being offended or rebellious, refusing to examine manipulation.
protestant-evangelical.12: A member reports manipulation, and leaders deny it, then accuse the member of gossip.
protestant-evangelical.13: Worship music, altar calls and dim lighting normalize emotional manipulation.
protestant-evangelical.14: Evangelical churches isolate through small groups, purity culture and Christian schooling.
protestant-evangelical.15: Evangelical churches triangulate through small groups and "concerned friends."
protestant-evangelical.16: After someone leaves, former friends and small-group members begin "checking in."
protestant-evangelical.17: Former members are described as offended, deconstructing, worldly or rebellious.
protestant-evangelical.18: A church says it handled a complaint "biblically," but refuses to disclose what happened.
protestant-evangelical.19: Altar calls manufacture consent through music, lighting and fear of eternal consequences.
protestant-evangelical.20: Evangelical spaces alternate intense fear and comfort: hell, purity shame, worship highs.
protestant-evangelical.21: A believer prays for healing, nothing changes, and they are told to pray harder.
protestant-evangelical.22: Evangelical churches often frame control as accountability: dating, giving, leadership.
protestant-evangelical.23: Adults are told to seek pastoral covering, submit to male headship and obey elders.
protestant-evangelical.24: Evangelical identity can become total: quiet time, purity, testimony and politics.
protestant-evangelical.26: Evangelical churches may push tithing, offerings, missions pledges and conferences.
protestant-evangelical.27: Evangelical spaces may manufacture crisis through rapture anxiety and persecution stories.
protestant-evangelical.28: Someone is praised as called or "on fire" until they burn out or question leadership.
protestant-evangelical.30: A church says membership is voluntary, but exit feels like rebellion.

shinto.1: Shinto draws people through festivals, shrines, purification rites and cultural belonging.
shinto.2: Shinto communities may offer festivals, purification rites and social cohesion.
shinto.3: Shinto future-fakes through purity, continuity, ancestral blessing and communal harmony.
shinto.4: A person distancing from shrine rites may be told they are disrespecting ancestors.
shinto.5: Shinto can devalue through purity, pollution, ancestral expectation and conformity.
shinto.6: A person declines shrine rites and hears, "It is not belief; it is respect."
shinto.7: Declining shrine rites is not religious dissent deserving protection but social defect.
shinto.8: Omikuji, omamori and shrine petitions pay out on chance, and winning visits are repeated.
shinto.9: A person attends family rituals "just for respect," then shrine visits are expected.
shinto.10: Shrine participation is "not religious" to skeptics, "disrespectful to refuse" to family.
shinto.11: A person refusing shrine rites may be accused of disrespect, impurity or coldness.
shinto.12: A person refuses shrine rites, and the family says, "It is just culture."
shinto.13: Shrine visits, festivals and ancestor observances become normal through repetition.
shinto.14: Shinto isolation can work through local shrine life, family rituals and conformity.
shinto.15: Shinto triangulation works through family, ancestors, kami, shrine and local community.
shinto.16: A person refusing shrine rites may be pressured by parents, grandparents and relatives.
shinto.17: A person refusing rituals may be smeared as cold, disrespectful, impure or selfish.
shinto.18: A person refuses shrine visits and family say, "It's just culture."
shinto.19: A person "chooses" shrine visits because refusal would be socially awkward.
shinto.20: A person feels pressure to participate in shrine rites, festivals and family rituals.
shinto.21: A person declines rituals and is told it is disrespectful, overthinking, or cold.
shinto.23: Adults may be told to participate because family and community expect it.
shinto.24: Identity is absorbed into family, ancestors, shrine, local community and seasonal rites.
shinto.26: Shinto financial control may be subtle: shrine donations and festival contributions.
shinto.27: Local pressures may manufacture crisis around ritual refusal or ancestor neglect.
shinto.28: A person who refuses shrine visits may be treated as cold or detached from roots.
shinto.30: Ritual participation is framed as "just culture," not religion; refusal is disrespect.

taoism.1: Seekers are attracted by effortless wisdom, nature, balance, qi and promised harmony.
taoism.2: Daoist teachers may offer healing rituals, qi practices, martial arts and balance.
taoism.3: Daoist-adjacent systems can future-fake through longevity, immortality, secret practices.
taoism.4: A student leaving a Daoist teacher may be told they are falling out of harmony.
taoism.5: Daoist-adjacent systems can devalue through claims the person is blocked or unbalanced.
taoism.7: Leaving the teacher is "forcing," and staying uncomfortable is "flow."
taoism.8: Energy practices pay out intermittently, and teachers explain both sensation and numbness.
taoism.9: A student of meditation or martial training then needs more forms and lineage access.
taoism.10: "Flow" can mean wise nonforce, but also passivity, obedience or surrender to a teacher.
taoism.11: A teacher may accuse a student of being blocked or rigid when the student resists control.
taoism.12: A student says a teacher is controlling, and the response may call the student blocked.
taoism.13: In controlling environments, obedience becomes "flow" and doubt becomes "resistance."
taoism.14: Daoist-adjacent groups can isolate through master-disciple hierarchy and secret teachings.
taoism.15: Daoist triangulation can work through master, lineage, qi diagnosis and "the Dao" itself.
taoism.16: A questioning student may be told, "You are not ready" or "You are disturbing harmony."
taoism.17: A student who leaves a teacher may be smeared as blocked, unbalanced or not ready.
taoism.18: A student questions a teacher's money and gets vague replies about timing and readiness.
taoism.19: A student "chooses" to trust a master after being told outsiders cannot judge it.
taoism.20: A teacher diagnoses a student as blocked, then offers correction or secret practice.
taoism.21: A student asks for clarity and receives poetry, paradox or claims they are not ready.
taoism.23: A teacher may describe students as not ready, too intellectual or energetically immature.
taoism.24: The student's identity may be redefined through flow, qi, lineage and master approval.
taoism.26: Daoist-adjacent teachers may charge for healing rituals, talismans, initiations, retreats.
taoism.27: Daoist-adjacent teachers may manufacture crisis through warnings about blocked qi.
taoism.28: A student who leaves a master may be labeled blocked, disharmonious or unready.
taoism.30: A master may say students are free to leave, while framing departure as blockage.
